**Dead Letters**

There is a room where the mail goes to fail.

No sign marks the door. Down a corridor that smells of wet wool and toner, past a bulletin board with a fire-safety notice from 1987, there is a steel door with no handle on the outside, and behind the door: the Dead Letter Office. I have worked here for nineteen years. My mother thinks I sort packages. I've never corrected her, because the truth sounds like eavesdropping, and eavesdropping sounds like theft, and I suppose in a way it is both.

Here is the job. When a letter cannot be delivered—address smudged past recovery, recipient moved without a trace, recipient dead with no forwarding soul—it comes to us. We open it. Not for pleasure; the manual is explicit on this point, in bold, twice. We open it to search for clues. A name in the signature block. A return address hidden in the folds. A postmark worth squinting at. Then we file it, hold it ninety days, and destroy it.

Most of what dies is dull. Bills chasing men who have changed cities like coats. Catalogues addressed to Previous Resident, a person who apparently lives everywhere and owns nothing. Birthday cards that missed by a year and now feel obscene. You learn to read fast and forget faster. You develop a kind of professional amnesia. If you kept everything, the room would fill with other people's lives, and there's barely room for your own.

But some letters come here because they were never going anywhere at all.

You can tell them by the weight. An envelope sealed with ceremony, stamped with care, addressed in handwriting that took its time—and inside, nothing but a name and a date, or no address whatsoever, just the words themselves, traveling to no one. Letters to fathers who died in March. Letters to sons who won't answer. Letters to God, which we're instructed to forward to Jerusalem, where someone agreed long ago to receive them. I imagine a wall of drawers somewhere holding our whole species' complaints and gratitude, and I hope somebody dusts it.

For years I processed those letters correctly. Opened, searched, filed, held, destroyed. Then, on a Tuesday in November—the month that seems designed for this work—I opened a letter with no address at all. The handwriting slanted left, pressed hard, the pen torn through in places. It began: *Dear Ruthie, You will be fifty this year. I still set the table wrong.*

I searched it for a clue, as trained. There was none. No surname, no city. Just a woman telling her sister about weather she couldn't share, a joke that needed explaining, an apology forty years old that she was making anyway, in case the mail worked differently than everyone said. At the bottom, beneath the signature: *I send this every year. I know where it goes. I like that it goes.*

Procedure said destroy after ninety days. I stood over my shredder with the manual open to that line, and my hands did something else. The letter went into my coat pocket, into my apartment, into a cigar box that until then had held only rubber bands and a dead watch battery.

Since then, the box has grown. I don't take often—maybe one letter in a hundred, only the ones clearly never meant to arrive, only the ones already addressed to no one living. A boy's report of his summer, mailed to a grandfather whose obituary was folded inside, as if the sender wanted the old man to have proof of himself. A recipe for plum cake with a note: *You always asked, and I always said it was a secret, but it was only that I didn't want to stop being the one who baked it.* A single page reading, in enormous child's letters, IM SORY, repeated down the margin like a fence.

People think letters are for delivering. Nineteen years in this room have taught me otherwise. The stamp is not the point. Writing is a way of speaking when speaking is impossible—to the dead, to the estranged, to the version of yourself who did the unforgivable thing. The envelope is just a body for the voice, and some voices aren't looking for ears. They're looking for a place to exist outside the skull. The mailbox is a kind of throat. Whatever happens downstream is weather.

My wife has been dead six years. I never wrote to her. I told myself I wasn't the type. But last Sunday I sat at my kitchen table with the good pen—the one in the box with the rubber bands—and I wrote her a letter. Nothing important. The radiator clanks in October. I still make the eggs the way you pretended to hate, soft, because it turns out I liked them soft. I have taken up keeping other people's unfinished business, and it has kept me.

I did not seal it. I did not stamp it. I certainly did not address it—she has no address now; she has everywhere, or nowhere, depending on which theology comforts you at 2 a.m., and I have tried several.

On Monday I put it in the cigar box, under the boy's summer and the plum cake and the apology forty years late, and I closed the lid. I want to tell you it felt like throwing a bottle into the sea, but the truth is smaller and better than that.

It felt delivered.

Letters to God, which we are instructed to forward to a church in Jerusalem that agreed decades ago to receive them; I imagine a wall of drawers somewhere holding all our species' complaints and gratitude, and I hope somebody dusts it.

For years I processed those letters correctly. Opened, searched, filed, held, destroyed. Then, on a Tuesday in November — the month that seems designed for this work — I opened a letter with no address at all. The handwriting was slanted left, pressed hard, the pen had torn through in places. It began: Dear Ruthie, You will be fifty this year. I still set the table wrong.

I searched it for a clue, as trained. There was none. No surname, no city. Just a woman telling her sister about the weather she couldn't share, a joke that needed explaining, an apology forty years old that she was making anyway, in case the mail worked differently than everyone said. At the bottom, beneath the signature, she had written: I send this every year. I know where it goes. I like knowing somewhere it goes.

Procedure said: destroy after ninety days. I read that line of the manual standing over my shredder, and my hands did something else. The letter went into my coat pocket, into my apartment, into a cigar box that had previously held only rubber bands and a dead watch battery.

Since then, the box has grown. I don't steal often — maybe one letter in a hundred, only the ones that were clearly never meant to arrive, only the ones already addressed to no one living. A boy's report of his summer, mailed to a grandfather whose obituary is folded inside as if the sender wanted the old man to have proof of himself. A recipe for plum cake with a note: You always asked, and I always said it was a secret, but it was only that I didn't want to stop being the one who baked it. A single page reading, in enormous child's letters, IM SORY, over and over down the margin like a fence.

People think letters are for delivering. Nineteen years in this room have taught me otherwise. The stamp is not the point. Writing is a way of speaking when speaking is impossible — to the dead, to the estranged, to the version of yourself who did the unforgivable thing. The envelope is just a body for the voice, and some voices aren't looking for ears. They're looking for a place to exist outside the skull. The mailbox is a kind of throat. What happens downstream is weather.

My wife has been dead six years. I never wrote to her. I told myself I wasn't the type. But last Sunday I sat at my kitchen table with the good pen, the one in the box with the rubber bands, and I wrote her a letter. Nothing important. The radiator clanks in October. I still make the eggs the way you hated, soft, because it turns out I liked them soft. I have taken up keeping other people's unfinished business and it has kept me.

I did not seal it. I did not stamp it. I certainly did not address it — she has no address; she has everywhere, or nowhere, depending on the theology you find comforting at 2 a.m., and I have tried several.

On Monday I put it in the cigar box, under the boy's summer and the plum cake and the apology forty years late, and I closed the lid, and I want to tell you that it felt like throwing a bottle into the sea, but the truth is smaller and better than that.

It felt delivered.
